A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same judge-tuning research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A-C are readable and can be matched despite pagination changes.

before.justification: v3 reports original judge-scaling experiments, evaluation of 4,480 configurations, benchmark results in Tables 2-4, and supplementary fidelity analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports a position-bias analysis relating response-order flip rate to human agreement.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B-C retain the same prompt and inference options, 4,480-configuration search, successive-halving procedure and accuracy/cost selection. Bias is additionally evaluated, but incorporating it into selection remains future work.

E1.justification: Both versions use Alpaca-Eval, Arena-Hard, LMSys and PandaLM test data. The added bias analysis examines existing judge configurations and response-order variations already present in the setup, without expanding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2-4 retain the same comparator membership within each experiment, including PandaLM, JudgeLM, Arena-Hard and the respective GPT/Claude judges and simple controls. The added related-work citations do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New Section 6 adds a diagnostic protocol measuring decision flips under response-order reversal and correlating flip rate with human agreement among top-rung configurations. Existing preprocessing, the 3,548/3,000 validation/test split, fidelity budgets and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds a targeted analysis asking whether accuracy/cost selection worsens position bias, using flip rate and human agreement. Existing hyperparameter, prompt-stability and fidelity analyses, including Figures 6, 7, 12 and 13, are retained.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains standard-deviation and coefficient-of-variation reporting, while Tables 2 and 4 retain their 100-bootstrap summaries. The new flip-rate correlation is a point estimate without additional run counts, uncertainty intervals or significance testing.

E6.justification: Table 3 changes PandaLM-7B human agreement from 0.60 to 0.62 under the same stated setting; Ours-small/medium/large remain 0.67/0.78/0.76. Section 6 newly reports r = -0.789 between flip rate and human agreement. Other matched results are unchanged.

T1.justification: The judge and metric equations in Section 3, tuning-cost derivations, and Pareto dominance and non-dominated sorting definitions in Appendix C are unchanged. The added empirical diagnostic introduces no mathematical derivation, formal assumption or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same scientific contributions: systematic judge analysis and economical multi-objective, multi-fidelity tuning yielding strong open-weight judges. The claimed tuning-cost advantage and main performance claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: Beyond v3's general bias caveats, v4 explicitly discusses biases omitted from selection, interprets the negative flip-rate correlation as no worsening of position bias, and warns that style/verbosity biases may worsen. Its Impact Statement also qualifies applicability to future models with new reasoning capabilities.

D1.justification: v3 promises a future code and annotation-data release. v4 supplies a repository address in the abstract and conclusion and states that these resources are released. Existing implementation, hardware, preprocessing and cost details in the appendices are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a prompt-optimization paragraph citing Zhou, Shi and Soylu et al. (2024), plus Liu et al. (2024) on alignment with human judgments. This modestly broadens context while retaining the existing novelty distinction around comprehensive judge tuning.

P1.justification: v4 adds a short related-work paragraph and standalone Limitations section, renumbers the conclusion, expands release and impact statements, and updates affiliation, contact, publication and funding text. Most existing prose and the overall narrative sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: All 13 numbered figures and six tables retain their designs and captions, with changed main-text placement: for example, Figure 3 moves from page 5 to 6 and Table 3 from page 8 to 7. Publication and funding graphics also change; appendix layouts match apart from pagination.

improvement.justification: v4 provides concrete code/data access information, a focused position-bias diagnostic, and clearer method-specific and future-model limitations than v3. These are useful, limited gains. The claim that selection does not worsen position bias exceeds what the reported correlation alone establishes, tempering the benefit; the main experiments and appendices otherwise remain unchanged.
